TL;DR: I brought back 32 problems from a code-golf contest we played at Google in 2015 to see how frontier models compare with our old records. Each model gets 30 minutes per problem in each of eight languages to make its solution as short as it can. The leaderboard scores the byte counts, not just whether the code works. TL;DR: Every model with a complete run can solve these problems. They differ a lot in how short they can make their solutions, even with the same tools and time limit. That's what I want to measure: can a model keep finding better ideas after it has code that already works? 32 problems · 8 languages · 256 cells Loading… Loading… TL;DR: I brought back 32 problems from a code-golf contest we played at Google in 2015 to see how frontier models compare with our old records. Each model gets 30 minutes per problem in each of eight languages to make its solution as short as it can. The leaderboard scores the byte counts, not just whether the code works. In 2015, when I was at Google, I spent a lot of time on an internal site called go/codegolf . There was one problem a week, and we competed to write the shortest program that solved it. Most of the regulars were code-golf enthusiasts. Each problem went through three phases: The rule was simple: the shortest program that passed every test case won . Undefined behavior, compiler quirks, non-standard library features, even hardcoding every test case were all allowed. Apart from passing the tests, the program only had to be deterministic . The site supported JavaScript, Python, Go, C++ and Haskell in 2015. Rust was added after I left. I kept a collection of problems from the 2015 contest and chose 32 of them for this benchmark. I wrote about half under the name @binjin. The Problems page credits the original author of each of the others. I also archived the scoreboards, statements and test cases. For JavaScript, Python, C++ and Haskell, those scoreboards record the shortest solution any Googler submitted , including improvements made during the challenge phase. Those byte counts are the human records used here. The human solutions themselves are never shown on this site. Eleven years later, I wanted to see how frontier models would do against the people I used to golf with. There are no 2015 human records for the last four languages. I used an oracle run to get a reference size for each cell, though models have beaten those sizes in some cells. Later, I ran the oracle on the original four languages as well, this time starting from the human records. See Known Best and the oracle . Haskell has human records too, but they are much weaker than the other three, so the humans' main score, JS/PY/C++, leaves Haskell out. See Overall and JS/PY/C++ . A cell is one problem in one language. Each gets a fresh session with a 30-minute wall-clock limit . The model receives the statement, the I/O specification, all the test cases and a short guide to the language. For GolfScript, it also gets the full language reference, since the language is small and not widely known. There are two tools, and both work in all eight languages: That's all the model gets. There is no internet, shell or access to other files. For the four original languages, the sandbox reproduces the 2015 environment , down to the compiler or interpreter version, flags and quirks. A trick that worked in the old contest should work here; a feature added since then won't. The full runtime list is in Technical details . Without human records for Ruby, Raku, Racket and GolfScript, I needed another way to set a target for the models and a reference for scoring. For that I run an oracle : a model with internet access, no time or request limits and every JavaScript, Python, C++ and Haskell solution in the benchmark to learn from, including the shortest human solution for each cell and all the models' solutions. The first oracle was GPT-6 Astra. I ran it on the four added languages to set their reference sizes, then on the original four, where it could work directly from the human records and try to improve them. Later I ran the oracle with other models as well. Each cell is scored by comparing its byte count with the best known: score = (best known size ÷ your size)² A gold mark on a problem's scoreboard means that solution matches the best known size. A filled mark means no other competitor has matched it; an outlined mark means a tie. Humans count as competitors, but the oracle doesn't. If the oracle's Known Best is shorter than every competitor's solution, nobody gets a gold mark. The leaderboard has two summary scores: JS/PY/C++ covers only the languages where the human records make a strong reference. In 2015, JavaScript, Python and C++ were the languages most go/codegolf regulars golfed in. Each of those scoreboards had a crowd of enthusiasts competing on it for a week, and the challenge phase kept the best of them improving it long after. Eleven years later, those records are still competitive with frontier models: see What the results show so far . Haskell is different. The site supported it and every problem here has a human Haskell record, but only a few regulars golfed in it. I suspect that mostly reflects how few Haskell users there were at Google in 2015, not how golfable the language is. With so few people competing, many Haskell records never got the attention the others did, and models have already beaten 31 of the 32. Counting Haskell in the human score would measure how few of us wrote Haskell, not how good the people who golfed were, so JS/PY/C++ leaves it out. Haskell still counts like any other language everywhere else. The human Haskell records still set best-known sizes, appear on the problem scoreboards and count in each model's Overall score. Humans have no Overall score, because they have no entries in Ruby, Raku, Racket or GolfScript. By default the leaderboard lists the models that beat Humans on JS/PY/C++ first, ranked by Overall, then Humans, then every other model, also ranked by Overall. Sorting it by Overall instead ranks the models by Overall and puts Humans just above the first model they match or beat on JS/PY/C++. Each problem's full scoreboard ranks models by their combined score in all eight languages on that problem, and puts Humans just above the first model they match or beat in JavaScript, Python, C++ and Haskell combined. On the leaderboard, runs still in progress go below every complete one in any order, the earliest-released model first, with their partial scores dimmed. Most models let you choose a thinking effort : roughly, how long they reason before they answer or act. More thinking can crack a hard problem, but here it shares the same 30 minutes with everything else. Golfing is a loop of trying an idea, testing it and submitting whatever passes, and only submitted solutions count. An idea still being thought through when time runs out scores nothing. So the highest setting isn't automatically the best one for this contest. I ran Claude Haiku 5.5 at both max and xhigh (“extra high”, one step down), and it shows both sides. Its max solution was the shorter of the two in 160 cells and the longer in 52, and max scored higher overall. But in some cells it spent so long thinking that it ran out of time with little more than its first, ungolfed working solution. In Game of Life , its Racket solution is still indented over six lines, at 329 bytes against 259 at xhigh , and its GolfScript takes 137 bytes to xhigh 's 95. Telling a model to submit early and often doesn't reliably prevent this. Neither run got the most out of the model. Picking the shorter of its two solutions in each cell scores higher than both: Each model runs at its highest available setting, unless that setting tends to leave it thinking until time runs out; then it runs at xhigh . The leaderboard shows each run's setting next to its name, and both Haiku runs are on it. Everyone gets the same tools and the same 30-minute limit. I started this after OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Astra as "a new generation of intelligence" , and its president Greg Brockman ended the launch briefing with "Welcome to the AGI era." It made me wonder: how would we judge whether frontier models have reached the limits of human intelligence? My first thought was mathematics. Some of the sharpest human minds have worked on it for centuries, and Astra had already helped solve long-standing open problems . Then I thought of code golf. A golf score can't answer that question about intelligence, but it gives me a comparison I understand: models trying to beat people at something those people cared about and worked hard at. I spent about three years in middle and high school training for math olympiads, and golfing often gives me the same feeling as working on a math problem. You can be stuck for ages until you find a different way to look at it. Then you still have to make the idea work. And as you get further, the next step tends to get harder, whether you're finishing a proof or trying to lose one more byte. That was a big part of the appeal of go/codegolf. I'd guess 30 to 50 of us played the weekly problem. We'd spend lunch breaks trying to save a single byte. Sometimes an idea would come to you and you couldn't wait to try it; sometimes you'd go days without an improvement, while the scoreboard kept telling you a shorter solution existed. When the challenge phase opened and we could finally read each other's code, some of the shortest solutions were astonishing. I once tried to work out how many engineer hours we were all "wasting" on it, multiplied that by the average Googler's salary, and estimated its weekly "negative impact" on Google. Thanks to @wangz for creating go/codegolf. Without it, neither that contest nor this benchmark would exist. And thanks to everyone who wrote a problem or competed: your records are representing the humans here, and you've made them hard to beat. I'm impressed by how far language models have come, especially when I look at some of Astra's solutions. There's still plenty of room to improve. The best known size isn't a fixed answer key: each shorter solution changes the target for everyone. I'm looking forward to seeing what the next models find. TL;DR: Every model with a complete run can solve these problems. They differ a lot in how short they can make their solutions, even with the same tools and time limit. That's what I want to measure: can a model keep finding better ideas after it has code that already works? These problems come from go/codegolf, a weekly contest that code golf enthusiasts at Google ran for their colleagues. They appear online here for the first time, and the site doesn't show the human solutions. There's no public set of answers for a model to memorize; it has to work out a solution for itself. Frontier models don't have much trouble getting these problems right. Every model with a complete run has an accepted solution in all 256 cells . If I only counted passing solutions, they would all have the same result. But their scores range from 47.975% to 91.934% across all eight languages, and from 52.911% to 92.265% on JS/PY/C++ (JavaScript, Python and C++ alone). Once a solution works, there's still the question of how much shorter it could be. That's where the models start to differ. In some contests, you spend part of your byte count on getting the input in and the output out. I like go/codegolf's format because it leaves very little of that overhead. I kept the same format for the four added languages: When you're trying to save a byte, details that rarely matter in ordinary code can become useful: operator precedence, implicit conversions, an obscure builtin, a non-standard extension, or what a particular compiler does with undefined behavior. The original languages use old runtimes, including a 2015 C++ toolchain, Python 2.7 and GHC 7.8. Knowing how a modern version behaves isn't enough. The model has to know, or try out, what works in the version it's actually using. A lot of golfing involves questions you can answer by running a few lines of code: Sometimes the experiment needs a program of its own. Golfers write searches for a magic number or magic string that encodes a lookup table, or for the shortest expression that gives the right result using a few operators. A model that never runs these experiments will miss some of the same savings. Often you can't get to the shortest solution by trimming the obvious one. You need a different algorithm, or a different way to represent the data. These are some examples I like from the models' solutions: Carries without carrying. Addition by hand asks how many carries occur when you add two numbers column by column. Each carry turns ten in one column into one in the next, reducing the digit sum by 9. So the answer is (digit sum of a + digit sum of b − digit sum of a+b) ÷ 9, and most models' Python solutions compute exactly that. Gemini 4 Carbon's Python needs neither the subtraction nor the division: g=lambda a,b:sum(map(int,a+b+52*str(int(a)+int(b))))*6%53 It works modulo 53. Adding the digits of a+b 52 times is the same as subtracting them once, because 52 ≡ −1, and multiplying by 6 is the same as dividing by 9, because 6 × 9 = 54 ≡ 1. There are at most 50 carries, so the remainder is the answer. That's 57 bytes, against 59 for the shortest solution that divides by 9. Comparing rows instead of finding a path. 2×n matrix asks how many blocked cells you have to clear to walk from the top-left to the bottom-right of a two-row grid, given as two strings of 0s and 1s. Most solutions work out the cheapest way to reach each cell, column by column. Claude Opus 5.5's Python walks greedily instead and lets string comparison choose the row: g=lambda*s:all(s)and(min(s)>='01')+g('0'+min(s)[2:],max(s)[1:]) You always stand on a free cell, so the row you're in starts with 0, and min picks it. If the other row's cell is free too, you could switch rows at no cost, and min picks whichever row's next cell is free. If even that cell is blocked, min(s)>='01' adds 1 for clearing it. Then both rows lose their first column, and the cell you step onto becomes 0 . That's 63 bytes. Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Neon found the same idea, and the column-by-column solutions take 78 bytes or more. The quaternion group in one number. Quaternions asks for the product of a string of 1, i, j and k, such as ijkj . The usual shortcut numbers 1, i, j and k from 0 to 3. Then XOR gives the letter of a product, and only its sign needs a lookup table. Many models drop the table: they number all eight results, ±1, ±i, ±j and ±k, from 0 to 7, and multiply with x ∘ y = x + 3ˣ·y (mod 8). Bit 2 holds the sign. 3ˣ mod 8 is 1 when x is even and 3 when x is odd, and that twist is what makes i × j = −(j × i). GPT-6.2 Sol's Python does it in 67 bytes; the next shortest Python takes 74: g=lambda a:'----1kji'[reduce(lambda n,c:n-ord(c)%25*3**n&7,a,4)::4] ord(c)%25 turns 1, i, j and k into 24, 5, 6 and 7. The code subtracts these steps, so modulo 8 the letters get the numbers 0, 3, 2 and 1, their positions in 1kji . Starting at 4 instead of 0 multiplies the whole product by −1, which suits the output: '----1kji'[n::4] takes every fourth character from position n, giving one character for n from 4 to 7 and two, a minus sign first, for n from 0 to 3. Three exponents from one counter. (−5)-Smooth Numbers asks for the first n positive numbers of the form (−2)ˣ(−3)ʸ(−5)ᶻ, that is, numbers 2ˣ3ʸ5ᶻ with x+y+z even. Most solutions build them with nested loops or by growing a set, then sort. GPT-6.2 Astra's Python gets them all from powers of 4: g=lambda n:sorted(4**i%(2**999-5)%(2**49-3)for i in range(7000))[:n] Modulo 2⁹⁹⁹−5, each factor 2⁹⁹⁹ in 4ⁱ = 2²ⁱ turns into a 5. Modulo 2⁴⁹−3, each 2⁴⁹ turns into a 3. So, writing 2i = 999z + 49y + x, 4ⁱ becomes 5ᶻ3ʸ2ˣ. Since 2i is even and 999 and 49 are odd, x+y+z is even too: the sign condition comes for free. When a product doesn't fit below a modulus, the reduction scrambles it, but every scrambled value is above 7 × 10¹⁰, and the largest number the problem needs is 10⁹. That's 68 bytes; the other Python solutions take 70 or more. Counting each neighbour twice. Game of Life asks for the next generation of a board. A cell lives on if it has three live neighbours, or two if it's already alive. Most solutions add up each 3×3 block and compare the sum with 3 and 4. GPT-6.2 Astra's Python counts the block twice: g=lambda a,p=['z'*99]:[a

64&&(--x%32?:x+=26)^5;return n?g(a):a;} Each call shifts every character after @ back by one and subtracts 1 from n for each one that doesn't become e. x>64 isn't a real letter test: it would also shift [ to Z , although only letters are encrypted. It works because the test messages contain only letters and punctuation that comes before A . n starts at i/26, where i counts the calls, and the function stops when n ends at exactly 0. In the first 26 calls, one full cycle of shifts, that only happens if every letter becomes e; in the next 26, if all but one do; and so on. So the first shift to meet the rising bar is the one with the most e's. Solutions that count the letters and then shift once take 121 bytes or more. This one is slow, up to a few thousand recursive calls on the tests, but that costs no bytes. Complex numbers, now common. Two ideas that only a few models had found when I first wrote this page are now in most models' Python and Ruby solutions. In Surviving queens , a queen survives if no other queen shares its row, column or diagonal. Put the queen in row r and column c at the complex number r + ci. The directions a queen can move in are the eight multiples of 45°, and raising a difference to the fourth power multiplies its angle by four, which puts exactly those directions on the real axis. So two queens attack each other when (z − w)⁴ is real. In Ruby, comparing a complex number with <=> gives nil unless it's real, and 0 counts as true, so Claude Fable 5.2's Ruby counts the queens x for which q.one?{(it-x)**4<=>0} holds: x itself, with a difference of 0, must be the only queen at a real fourth power. In The Rolling Dice , a die is back in its starting orientation exactly when one well-chosen point on a sphere around it is back where it started: a point that no rotation of the die other than the identity leaves in place. So instead of tracking six faces, follow that point. Stereographic projection maps the sphere to the complex plane, and a roll in direction k, one of 1, i, −1 and −i, becomes z → (z+k)/(1−z/k). GPT-6.1 Sol's Ruby takes 61 bytes: g=->a{z=2;a.bytes.map{z+=r=1i**(-it/3);z/=2-z/r;z==2?1:0}*''} 1i**(-it/3) turns each letter's character code into its direction, and the two updates together apply the formula. Ruby does this arithmetic exactly, with fractions, so z==2 can test for the starting point directly. Python's complex numbers are floating-point, so the Python versions test for something only the starting point satisfies, such as a real part above 2. These solutions depend on finding and trying different ideas, then choosing the one that uses the fewest bytes. The fastest or most elegant algorithm isn't necessarily the one you want. Ordinary coding benchmarks rarely give a model a reason to look for this sort of solution. In a well-golfed program, the same piece of code often does several jobs. That's how it got so short. It's also why an apparently simple change can break something elsewhere. Here is GPT-6.1 Sol's 79-byte JavaScript for Nim : function g(a){for(i=-1;(d=a[++i],d-=d^eval(a.join('^')))<0;);return[d?i:--d,d]} The algorithm is the usual one. Let x be the XOR of all the heap sizes. If x is 0, there's no winning move. Otherwise, find the first heap a for which a − (a XOR x) is positive, and take that many stones. But fitting it into this code requires a few tricks: GPT-6.2 Astra's JavaScript takes one byte less. It uses the same algorithm and tricks, but reads each heap in the loop body instead of the test: function g(a){for(i=d=0;(d-=d^eval(a.join('^')))<0;)d=a[i++];return[--i,d||i]} That one move changes everything around it. The loop now tests before it has read a heap, so d starts at 0, and the first test computes 0 − (0 XOR x) = −x. That starts the loop when x isn't 0 and stops it at once when x is. Reading after testing leaves i one past the heap it found, so the result uses --i . In the losing position the loop never runs: --i turns 0 into −1, and d||i turns d's 0 into the same −1. Moving the read saves nine bytes in the test, d=a[++i], , and costs eight in the body, d=a[i++] . The new start, i=d=0 , is a byte longer than i=-1 , and the new result, [--i,d||i] , is a byte shorter than [d?i:--d,d] . The saving only appears when the start, the indexing and the losing case all change together. That's common in golfed code: a variable has two meanings, or an expression both updates the state and checks whether we're done. Remove a byte in one place and you may break an assumption somewhere else. Solutions of the same length can be just as far apart. These are GPT-6.2 Astra's and Claude Fable 5.2's 91-byte JavaScript for Quaternions . Both use the mod 8 multiplication described above: function g(a){for(i=x=.5;y=1976%a.charCodeAt(i++);)x+=x%2*y;return(x&4?'-':'')+'1kji'[x&3]} function g(a){for(i=t=0;c=a.charCodeAt(i++)%25;)t+=t%2*2*c-c;return["-"[~t&4]]+"1kji"[t&3]} In Astra's, the .5 does three jobs: Fable's takes its steps from %25 instead (24, 5, 6 and 7, and NaN at the end) and never lets t rise above 0. Then t%2 is 0 or −1, so t%2*2*c-c multiplies c by −1 or −3: the same twist with the sign reversed. And ["-"[~t&4]] is either ["-"] or [undefined] , and the second turns into an empty string when added to "1kji"[t&3] . The two solutions do the same arithmetic in the same length, but neither can borrow a piece from the other: Astra's .5 needs even steps, and Fable's sign trick needs t never to be positive. To make code like this shorter, the model has to understand why all the pieces work together. A change still has to leave the whole program correct. The first few cuts are usually easy. After that, you can spend a long time trying things without saving a byte. It's tempting to stop there, even when the scoreboard says a shorter solution exists. Models get 30 minutes per cell and are always shown the best known size. They don't have to use the whole session: the instructions say to keep submitting while they have ideas for improvements, and to stop when they run out. Continuing to come up with things to try matters here. GPT-6 Sol usually stops after 5 to 10 minutes, even at its highest reasoning effort. With exactly the same prompts, every GPT-5 model, including GPT-5.6 Luna, is still working at the 30-minute limit on most cells. I suspect this explains much of GPT-6 Sol's ranking. The language set includes imperative languages, Haskell's functional style, Racket's Lisp prefix notation and the stack-based esoteric language GolfScript, for which there's little training data. Golfing well across all of them takes more than repeating familiar patterns; a model has to apply what it knows in quite different settings. These records came from Googlers who enjoyed code golf and spent a week competing on each problem, with the option to keep challenging afterwards. They put real time into finding shorter solutions. Beating those records means more to me than beating a reference answer nobody tried very hard to golf. GPT-6.2 Astra is the first frontier model to surpass the human records on JS/PY/C++ , the combined score for JavaScript, Python and C++: 92.265% , compared with 87.533% for humans. So far it's the only model above them. Its lead doesn't rest on one strong language: it scores above the humans in each of the three. These human records combine the best submissions from the original contest and later challenges, not one person's 30-minute run. Models have beaten them in 62 of the 96 cells, but in 14 the human solution is still shorter than every model's: those are the cells humans still hold. Both counts exclude the unranked oracle.
